point.competitive: **Positive and negative pressure are both tools for imposing your agenda.** Lure moves the opponent toward your position by attraction. Threat moves them by compulsion. The result is the same: they are reacting to you.

point.gentle: **Water does not have a fixed form, yet it always reaches the low ground.** The right approach depends on this specific opponent in this specific moment, not on what worked before.
point.direct: **Do not repeat tactics that have already won a victory.** The opponent adapts, and repeating a method turns a once-effective surprise into a predictable signal.
point.competitive: **Formlessness is the highest tactical discipline.** Every pattern you repeat teaches the opponent how to defeat you. The commander who can modify methods in relation to the specific opponent is the one who cannot be anticipated.

oneMinuteRecap.gentle: Whoever arrives first sets the terms. Two mechanisms keep you from arriving second: offer what the opponent must come toward, or threaten what they cannot abandon. And like water that has no fixed shape but always finds the low ground, the right tactics depend on this specific opponent in this specific moment, not on what succeeded before.
oneMinuteRecap.direct: First-in-field sets the terms; the latecomer responds on someone else's prepared ground. Lure and threat achieve the same result by different means: both place the opponent on ground you chose rather than ground they would have selected. Do not repeat tactics; methods must be governed by the specific opponent and circumstances. The heaven-born captain is the one who modifies his approach in relation to what this moment actually requires.
oneMinuteRecap.competitive: First in the field is fresh and sets terms. Second in the field is exhausted and responds. Two mechanisms impose the agenda. Formlessness denies the opponent a reliable pattern. Everything in the chapter is a consequence of who is shaping the contest and who is absorbing it.

activationPrompt.gentle: Before reading further, think of one ongoing contest where someone else is currently controlling the agenda. Not where you are behind, but where the terms were set before you arrived. What would it have taken to arrive first?
activationPrompt.direct: Identify one contest in your work or personal life where you are currently operating on terms you did not set. Name the specific mechanism that put the agenda in the other person's hands before your engagement began.
activationPrompt.competitive: Name one active contest where you are reacting rather than setting terms. Diagnose whether the agenda-control failure is a first-in-field problem, a lure-and-threat problem, or a knowledge-asymmetry problem. Then name what a reversal would require.

chapterBreakdown.gentle:
An exhausted messenger arrives at a ridge after three hours in the rain, and a commander is already there, rested, with tents pitched and water boiling. The messenger is not less skilled. He arrived second, and second means accepting ground someone else chose. Sun Tzu opens the chapter on that asymmetry. Whoever arrives first sets the terms, controls the ground, and determines what the engagement will be about. The latecomer responds on terrain he did not select, at a pace someone else established.

From this opening, Sun Tzu develops two mechanisms for ensuring you set the terms rather than inheriting them. The first is positive: offer what the opponent must come toward. Draw them onto your prepared ground by giving them a reason they cannot refuse. The second is negative: threaten what they cannot afford to ignore. Force them to respond to a danger that directs them away from their own intended agenda and toward your prepared position. Both mechanisms work by making the opponent move toward you, rather than requiring you to move toward them.

The chapter then turns to the knowledge problem. Discover your opponent's dispositions while concealing your own. That asymmetry, knowing more than you reveal, produces the structural advantage that allows concentration. If you know where the opponent is thin and they cannot read where you are thick, you can bring your whole strength against their divided fractions. The knowledge gap is what makes concentration possible.

Two precise rules follow from that knowledge advantage. Attack only positions the opponent has left undefended. Defend only positions that cannot be attacked. The result, when both rules hold, is reliable success in both directions. Sun Tzu is not claiming perfect certainty in every engagement; he is claiming that selecting targets and selecting defensive positions by this criterion produces outcomes predictable enough to plan around.

The chapter closes with the water metaphor: no constant shape, always flowing toward the low ground. Tactics should operate the same way. Repeating what succeeded in the first engagement signals to the opponent where the second will come from. The method that produced surprise in round one becomes the pattern the opponent builds a counter around in round two. The heaven-born captain is defined as the one who modifies methods in relation to the specific opponent and the specific circumstances, with no fixed form and no repeatable recipe. The practical difficulty of this standard is not technical but institutional. Methods that worked before are easy to justify, easy to communicate, and easy to defend. A method that worked before can be documented, trained, and repeated. A method modified for the specific opponent and moment cannot be planned in advance, which means the organization that requires advance sign-off on every tactical choice cannot produce the heaven-born captain's behavior even when a talented commander is present. The chapter sets a standard that demands real-time judgment at the point of contact, not procedural approval from above. Both are required.
chapterBreakdown.direct:
Sun Tzu opens by distinguishing two kinds of arrival. First in the field means arriving fresh, with time to prepare the ground and set the terms of engagement. Second in the field means arriving exhausted, on terrain chosen by someone else, responding to conditions already established. The asymmetry is structural: the first-in-field commander is imposing will; the latecomer is absorbing it. Imposing your will is the active discipline. Preventing the opponent from imposing theirs is the defensive form of the same discipline.

From that principle, Sun Tzu derives two concrete mechanisms of agenda control. Lure: offer what the opponent must come toward. Make your prepared position attractive enough that the opponent moves toward it voluntarily. Threaten: target what the opponent cannot abandon. Make the cost of not responding to your initiative greater than the cost of responding, so the opponent redirects toward your preferred engagement point. Both mechanisms achieve the same structural result: the opponent is moving toward your position rather than setting their own.

Behind both mechanisms is a knowledge requirement. A commander who discovers the opponent's dispositions while concealing his own holds an asymmetry that makes concentration possible. Knowing which of the opponent's positions are actually thin, while keeping your own distribution opaque, allows you to bring a whole force against a fraction. Without that knowledge advantage, concentration is guesswork. The active work of intelligence-gathering and the active work of concealment are both required to maintain the asymmetry.

From the knowledge advantage, two targeting rules emerge. Attack only positions the opponent has left undefended; those are the positions where concentration wins reliably. Defend only positions the opponent cannot attack; those are the positions where you do not need to commit force to hold them. Together, the two rules produce reliable outcomes in both directions by restricting commitment to situations where the terms are already favorable.

The chapter closes on the water image. Water flows toward the low ground without a fixed shape, adapting to the actual terrain rather than following a fixed route. Tactics must work the same way. Every method that produced a victory reveals information about your approach to the opponent who adapts. Repeating the method turns a surprise into a signal. The heaven-born captain is defined precisely as the one who modifies methods in relation to the specific opponent, with no fixed form and no repeatable recipe. The failure mode this defines is not incompetence but habit. The commander who repeats a successful method is not making an irrational choice — the method worked before and repetition is lower-risk than improvisation under pressure. Sun Tzu's argument is that this calculation is wrong under adversarial conditions precisely because the success was visible to the opponent. Every repeated method provides the opponent with an additional observation, and each observation narrows the range of responses the opponent needs to prepare. The heaven-born captain's advantage is not cleverness — it is denying the opponent the information that repeated methods unavoidably generate.
chapterBreakdown.competitive:
Sun Tzu's sixth chapter is built on a single asymmetry: whoever arrives first sets the terms, and the latecomer arrives exhausted on ground he did not choose. That asymmetry is not just about physical positioning. It is about who is imposing will and who is absorbing it. The commander who sets the terms is running the active form of strategic discipline. The commander who responds to terms set by the other side is running the defensive form, and Sun Tzu treats that as already behind.

Two mechanisms operationalize the active form. Positive pressure: offer what the opponent must come toward. Construct the engagement so that the opponent's own rational interests direct them toward your prepared position. Negative pressure: threaten what they cannot afford to ignore. Force a response that redirects the opponent away from their own agenda and toward yours. Both mechanisms move the opponent; neither requires you to chase them. The active commander does not need to catch the opponent. He places the engagement so that the opponent arrives.

Behind both mechanisms is a knowledge asymmetry. Discover the opponent's dispositions while concealing yours. That gap is what makes concentration possible. A commander who knows where the opponent is thin and keeps his own distribution concealed can bring his whole force against their divided fractions, not because he has more total strength but because he has it in the right place at the right moment while the opponent does not. The active intelligence work and the active concealment work are inseparable from the concentration advantage.

From that knowledge advantage, two precise targeting rules emerge. Attack only what the opponent has left undefended; that is where your concentration wins reliably. Defend only what the opponent cannot attack; that is where you do not need to commit force. Both rules restrict commitment to favorable terms rather than requiring a commander to fight on any ground the opponent chooses.

The chapter closes with the hardest principle: formlessness. Water flows to the low ground without a fixed shape, governed by the actual terrain rather than by habit. The commander who won by a specific method has revealed that method to every opponent who observed the result. Repeating the method gives the next opponent the information he needs to build a counter before the engagement begins. The heaven-born captain is defined as the one who modifies methods in relation to the specific opponent in the specific moment, with no fixed form and no repeatable recipe. That is the discipline, not the exception. The competitive advantage of method variation is not that it is clever. It is that an opponent cannot build a counter to a method he has not yet observed. Each novel approach forces the opponent to respond to what is actually happening rather than to what he has prepared for. The commander who maintains form variation across engagements accumulates a growing gap between what the opponent expects and what actually arrives. The opponent cannot.

moreDetails.gentle: The agenda-control principle has a limit that does not appear in the basic version. Luring the opponent onto your prepared ground requires having something to spare: resources, time, or position that allows you to extend an offer without depleting your own readiness. When your resources are already fully committed, the lure can expose your position before the engagement rather than drawing the opponent into it. The mechanism works most reliably when there is genuine slack in your situation; it becomes dangerous when every commitment is already at its maximum.
moreDetails.direct: The lure mechanism carries a boundary condition: it requires a resource surplus sufficient to absorb the cost of placing bait without depleting your own position. If your resources are equal to the opponent's or inferior, luring them onto your ground may reveal your position before the engagement rather than securing the advantage. The lure works when you have something genuinely to spare. It fails when every commitment is already extended, because the preparation the lure requires becomes a vulnerability the opponent can exploit before arriving.
moreDetails.competitive: Agenda control has a threshold that the principle does not advertise. Imposing your will through the lure mechanism requires absorbing the cost of that imposition, which means a resource surplus that allows you to extend an offer without simultaneously revealing a gap. If your resources are equal to the opponent's or inferior, the lure exposes your investment before the opponent commits. The mechanism is powerful against an opponent who has less information about your actual position; it is dangerous when the opponent can read your commitment level from the preparation itself.

point.gentle: **Imposing your will is the active form; not allowing theirs to be imposed is the defensive form.** Both require you to shape who moves toward whom rather than accepting the terms the other side establishes.
point.direct: **Imposing will is the active form of the discipline; preventing the opponent from imposing theirs is the defensive form.** The two mechanisms, lure and threat, both work by making the opponent move toward your prepared position rather than forcing you to respond to theirs.
point.competitive: **The active discipline is imposing your agenda; the defensive form is denying them theirs.** Two mechanisms accomplish this: offer what they must come for, or threaten what they cannot abandon. Both move the opponent toward you.

moreDetails.gentle: The concentration-versus-division advantage has a timing problem that the principle does not resolve. If you concentrate your force before the opponent has divided, the act of concentration itself can be observed and read. The chapter assumes you can discover the opponent's dispositions without being read in return. When both sides are actively concealing their own dispositions and trying to discover the other's, the first commander to commit to concentration has also revealed information. The advantage belongs to whichever side has better intelligence at the moment of commitment, not simply to whichever side concentrates.
moreDetails.direct: The concentration-vs-division dynamic has a timing vulnerability. Concentrating your force before the opponent's division is established can be detected and used by the opponent to counter the concentration. The principle assumes you can read the opponent's distribution without being read in return. In situations where both sides are actively concealing dispositions and gathering intelligence, the first commitment to concentration is also an information disclosure. The advantage is available to the side with more reliable intelligence at the decisive moment, not simply to the side that concentrates.
moreDetails.competitive: The concentration-versus-division advantage rests on an intelligence asymmetry that cannot be assumed in a contested environment. Both sides are actively trying to discover the other's dispositions while concealing their own. The first side to commit concentration has revealed the fact of concentration and roughly where it is directed. The advantage is available to the side whose intelligence is more reliable at the moment of commitment, not simply to the side that concentrates first. Concentrating on bad intelligence against an opponent who has read your movement is worse than not concentrating at all.

point.gentle: **Discover the opponent's dispositions while concealing yours.** That knowledge asymmetry is what allows you to concentrate your whole force against their divided fractions rather than guessing where to commit.
point.direct: **The knowledge asymmetry between discovered dispositions and concealed ones produces a structural concentration advantage.** A commander who reveals his dispositions while trying to discover the opponent's has inverted the advantage.
point.competitive: **Knowledge asymmetry is the mechanism behind concentration.** Knowing where the opponent is thin while keeping your own distribution opaque allows whole-force commitment against a fraction. Revealing your dispositions while trying to discover theirs hands that advantage to the opponent.

moreDetails.gentle: Selecting undefended positions as targets is harder than it sounds, because undefended positions are not always undefended for the reason you want. Some positions are undefended because the opponent judged them strategically irrelevant. Attacking an irrelevant position is not a concentration advantage; it is a misdirection of your own effort. The principle requires knowing which gaps in the opponent's coverage are gaps that matter strategically, not just which positions happen to be empty. And over time, consistently attacking certain undefended positions reveals to the opponent which positions you consider worth attacking, which teaches them your own map of what matters.
moreDetails.direct: The selection problem for 'attack undefended' runs in two directions. First, an undefended position may be undefended because the opponent considers it irrelevant, which means attacking it produces no strategic gain and wastes the concentration advantage. Second, the pattern of which positions you select as targets teaches the opponent which positions you believe are strategically significant, and therefore which positions you consider well-defended and therefore avoided. Consistent application of the principle reveals your disposition map through the pattern of your choices even when you never defend or attack the same position twice.
moreDetails.competitive: The selection problem for 'attack undefended' has a deeper layer. An undefended position may be undefended because the opponent assessed it as unimportant, making an attack on it a waste of concentration. But more critically, a commander who consistently attacks certain classes of undefended positions signals to the opponent which positions he considers strategically significant, and therefore reveals which positions he would also defend, and which he would avoid. Formlessness requires not repeating which positions you treat as the threshold of strategic relevance, not only not repeating the specific tactic used to attack them.

point.gentle: **Attack only what has been left undefended; defend only what cannot be attacked.** Selecting by these two criteria produces reliable outcomes in both directions by restricting commitment to already-favorable terms.
point.direct: **Certainty of success in attack and defense comes from restricting commitment to positions already favorable.** Attack only undefended positions; defend only positions the opponent cannot attack. The principle is about selection, not about force level.
point.competitive: **Attack only undefended positions; defend only inattackable ones.** The selection discipline is what produces reliable outcomes. Committing force to contested positions on unfavorable terms is the failure mode the principle exists to prevent.

chapterBreakdown.gentle:
Imagine a position on a hillside above a narrow valley, occupied by the time the sun rises. Down in the valley, troops arrive hours later, winded, not knowing the terrain, with no time to prepare. The commander on the hill did not defeat them in battle. He defeated them by arriving first. Sun Tzu opens the chapter on that gap. First in the field means arriving fresh, with time to prepare the ground and frame what the contest will be about. Second in the field means arriving already depleted, on terrain someone else already knows.

From that opening, Sun Tzu offers two practical mechanisms for ensuring you are always the one who arrives first in conceptual terms. The first is positive: offer what the opponent must come toward. Give them a reason they cannot decline, and they will move toward your prepared position. The second is negative: threaten what they cannot afford to abandon. Force a response that redirects them away from their own agenda and toward your chosen engagement point. A skilled commander does not wait for the engagement to begin and then try to respond. He shapes the situation so that the opponent's rational choices all lead toward a position already prepared.

Behind both mechanisms is a knowledge requirement. You must discover the opponent's dispositions while concealing your own. That asymmetry allows you to concentrate your full force against fractions of theirs, not because you have more strength in total, but because you know where they are thin while they cannot read where you are strong. The discovery is not passive; it requires active intelligence gathering. And the concealment is not automatic; it requires active effort to keep your own distribution opaque.

Two precise rules follow. Attack only positions the opponent has left undefended; that is where your concentration wins reliably. Defend only positions the opponent cannot attack; that is where you do not need to commit force. Together, these rules produce reliable outcomes by restricting commitment to already-favorable situations.

The chapter ends with an image that carries its own argument. Water has no constant shape. It flows around obstacles, fills whatever is low, finds its route by the actual terrain. Tactics must work the same way. What succeeded in the last engagement revealed your method. Repeating the method gives the opponent the pattern they need to counter you. Governing approach by the specific opponent and the specific moment is what the heaven-born captain does.
chapterBreakdown.direct:
Sun Tzu opens by naming a structural asymmetry. First in the field means arriving fresh, with time to prepare, choosing the ground, and setting the terms. Second in the field means arriving exhausted, on ground someone else prepared, responding to conditions already established. The difference between the two is not a matter of relative skill or courage at the moment of engagement. It is a product of who controlled the timing. Imposing your will is the active form of the discipline. Not allowing the opponent to impose theirs is the defensive form of the same discipline.

From that principle, Sun Tzu derives two agenda-control mechanisms. Lure: offer what the opponent must come toward, so that their own rational interests direct them to your prepared position. Threat: target what they cannot abandon, forcing a response that redirects them away from their own agenda. Both mechanisms move the opponent toward you rather than requiring you to chase them. The skilled commander uses both selectively depending on which the situation supports.

The knowledge requirement behind both mechanisms is explicit in the chapter. Discovering the opponent's dispositions while concealing your own produces an asymmetry that makes concentration possible. A commander who knows where the opponent is thin, while keeping his own distribution opaque, can bring a whole force against a fraction. A commander who reveals his own dispositions while trying to discover the opponent's has inverted the advantage entirely.

From that knowledge advantage, two targeting rules emerge. Attack only undefended positions; that is where concentration wins reliably. Defend only positions that cannot be attacked; that is where commitment is not required. Both rules work by restricting engagement to situations where the terms are already favorable before the commitment is made.

The chapter closes on the water principle. Water has no constant shape but always flows to the low ground. Tactics must be governed by the specific opponent and specific circumstances rather than by habit. Repeating a successful method reveals the approach and removes the surprise that made it effective. The heaven-born captain is defined as the one who modifies methods in relation to the specific opponent, with no fixed form.
chapterBreakdown.competitive:
First in the field is fresh; second in the field is exhausted and responding on someone else's terms. That asymmetry is the foundation of the entire chapter. Sun Tzu frames it as a discipline with two forms. The active form is imposing your will on the engagement. The defensive form is preventing the opponent from imposing theirs. Both require you to control who moves toward whom.

Two mechanisms operationalize that control. Positive: offer what the opponent must come toward. Construct the situation so that their own rational interests drive them toward your prepared position. Negative: threaten what they cannot abandon. Make the cost of not responding greater than the cost of responding, which redirects their attention and movement. The skilled commander does not pick one approach as a style. He applies whichever one the situation supports, and switches between them as the opponent adapts.

The knowledge requirement is embedded in both mechanisms. You must know where the opponent is actually thin, and they must not know where you are actually thick. That asymmetry is what makes concentration possible. Concentrate your whole against their divided fractions, not because you have more in total, but because you know where to apply what you have while they do not know where you will. A commander who reveals his dispositions while gathering intelligence on the opponent's has surrendered the advantage before the concentration begins.

Two targeting rules follow directly. Attack only what the opponent has left undefended; that is where your concentration produces a reliable outcome. Defend only positions the opponent cannot attack; that is where you do not need to spend force. Both rules restrict commitment to already-favorable terms.

Formlessness closes the chapter. Water flows to the low ground without a fixed shape, governed by the terrain rather than by habit or precedent. Every method that produced a victory has taught the opponent something about your approach. Repeating it converts surprise into signal. The heaven-born captain governs methods by the specific opponent in the specific moment, with no repeatable recipe and no fixed form.

moreDetails.gentle: The two mechanisms of agenda control, lure and threat, both depend on the opponent moving toward you rather than you chasing them. Lure works by making your position attractive; threat works by making any other position costly. Either way, you are not scrambling to catch up. You have already prepared the ground, and the opponent's choices all lead toward it. The practical problem is identifying which mechanism fits which opponent. An opponent who is driven by acquisition responds to lure. An opponent who is driven by fear of loss responds to threat. Reading which is true is part of the intelligence work the chapter requires.
moreDetails.direct: The two agenda-control mechanisms operate through different motivational levers. Lure works by giving the opponent a reason to move toward your position because of what they stand to gain. Threat works by giving the opponent a reason to move toward your position because of what they stand to lose. Both achieve the same structural result: you are not responding to their agenda; they are responding to yours. The selection between lure and threat is itself a strategic judgment that requires reading the opponent's actual motivational structure, not just their stated priorities.
moreDetails.competitive: Lure and threat are not interchangeable. Lure works on opponents driven by acquisition; threat works on opponents driven by loss-aversion. Applying the wrong one wastes the initiative. A threat that does not target something the opponent genuinely cannot afford to lose is just noise. A lure that does not offer something the opponent genuinely must pursue is just bait they will walk past. Reading which mechanism fits which opponent is itself an intelligence problem, and getting it wrong hands the opponent the response time you were trying to deny them.

point.gentle: **Imposing your will is the active form of agenda control; preventing the opponent's will from being imposed is the defensive form.** Both require shaping who moves toward whom rather than accepting whatever terms emerge from the contest.
point.direct: **The active form of strategic discipline is imposing your will; the defensive form is denying the opponent's.** Two mechanisms, lure and threat, both work by making the opponent move toward your prepared position rather than requiring you to respond to theirs.
point.competitive: **Agenda control runs in two directions: impose your will, and prevent the opponent from imposing theirs.** The two mechanisms, lure and threat, both accomplish this by moving the opponent toward your position rather than yours toward theirs.

moreDetails.gentle: Discovering the opponent's dispositions is not passive observation. It requires active work: probing, sending scouts, creating situations that force the opponent to respond in ways that reveal their positions. And maintaining concealment is not just staying quiet. It requires actively managing what signals you send and ensuring that the opponent's intelligence-gathering produces an inaccurate picture of your distribution. Both halves of the asymmetry require ongoing effort, and the effort on both sides is being opposed by the opponent's countermeasures.
moreDetails.direct: Paragraphs 13 and 14 make explicit that the discovery function is active, not passive. You cannot simply observe the opponent's dispositions from a distance and assume the picture is accurate. The chapter implies that the opponent is also actively concealing, which means the intelligence-gathering requires active probing rather than passive surveillance. A commander who treats discovery as watching and treats concealment as silence has already given the opponent's counter-intelligence operation an easier target than a commander who actively shapes what the opponent sees.
moreDetails.competitive: The knowledge-asymmetry principle has a two-front structure. Discovery requires active probing that forces the opponent to reveal dispositions through their responses. Concealment requires actively shaping the signals you project so the opponent's intelligence picture is inaccurate rather than just incomplete. A commander who passively observes while staying quiet has not built an asymmetry; he has produced mutual opacity, which benefits whichever side has better pre-existing intelligence rather than whichever side is more disciplined about discovery and concealment.

point.gentle: **Discover the opponent's dispositions while concealing yours.** That knowledge gap allows you to concentrate your whole strength against their divided fractions rather than spreading to match whatever they might do.
point.direct: **The knowledge asymmetry between discovered dispositions and concealed ones produces the structural advantage that makes concentration possible.** A commander who reveals his own dispositions while trying to discover the opponent's has inverted the advantage.
point.competitive: **Knowledge asymmetry is the mechanism behind concentration.** Knowing where the opponent is thin while keeping your own distribution opaque allows you to bring whole-force commitment against a fraction, regardless of total strength.

moreDetails.gentle: Undefended positions are not all equal in strategic value. Some positions are undefended because the opponent considered them irrelevant. Attacking an irrelevant position uses your concentration without producing any strategic outcome. The principle asks you to identify which undefended positions actually matter, which requires the same intelligence work as identifying where the opponent is thin. The selection problem is not solved by the principle; it is defined by it.
moreDetails.direct: The selection problem for the 'attack undefended' principle runs deeper than identifying which positions happen to be unprotected. An undefended position may be undefended because the opponent judged it strategically unimportant. Attacking it produces no gain and depletes the concentration advantage. The principle requires knowing which gaps in the opponent's coverage are strategically significant, and that knowledge requirement connects directly back to the intelligence work in the previous takeaway. The chapter names the rule without resolving how the selection is actually made.
moreDetails.competitive: The 'attack undefended' principle carries a selection problem the chapter does not fully resolve. Undefended positions may be undefended because they are irrelevant to the opponent's actual strategic position. Concentrating against an irrelevant gap wastes the advantage. The principle requires identifying which undefended positions are actually consequential, which is itself an intelligence problem that depends on understanding the opponent's actual priorities rather than just observing their force distribution.

point.gentle: **Attack only what the opponent has left undefended; defend only what cannot be attacked.** Restricting commitment to those situations produces reliable outcomes in both directions.
point.direct: **The certainty-of-success principle works through selection, not force level.** Attack only undefended positions; defend only inattackable ones. Both rules produce reliable outcomes by restricting engagement to already-favorable terms.
point.competitive: **Attack only undefended positions; defend only inattackable ones.** The selection discipline is what produces predictability in both directions. Committing force to contested ground on unfavorable terms is the failure mode these rules exist to prevent.

moreDetails.gentle: Paragraph 28 makes the formlessness principle concrete: do not repeat tactics that have already won a victory. The opponent observed what worked. Repeating the approach gives the opponent a map of where you will go next, which removes the surprise that made the first success possible. What worked once becomes a pattern; what becomes a pattern becomes a prediction; what can be predicted can be countered. The discipline is not to avoid tactics that work but to avoid making the method itself a fixed object the opponent can study.
moreDetails.direct: Paragraph 28 gives a specific mechanism for why formlessness matters: do not repeat tactics that have produced a victory, because the opponent adapts. The surprise that made the first method effective becomes, after one use, a data point the opponent uses to build a counter. A method that is used twice against the same or similar opponent is no longer surprising; it is a pattern. A pattern is information. Information in the opponent's hands is a resource against you. Formlessness is the discipline of denying the opponent that resource.
moreDetails.competitive: Paragraph 28 is explicit: do not repeat tactics that have won one victory. The opponent adapts after the first use. Repeating the method converts the surprise that produced the first success into a predictable signal that tells the opponent where the next attempt will come from. Every repeated method increases the opponent's intelligence advantage. Formlessness is not a style preference; it is the only discipline that denies the opponent the information compounding that repetition produces.

point.gentle: **Water has no constant shape but always finds the low ground.** Methods should be governed by the specific opponent and the circumstances, not by what has worked before or by personal preference.
point.direct: **Do not repeat tactics that have produced a previous victory.** The opponent adapts to what they have observed, and repeating the method removes the surprise that made it effective.
point.competitive: **Formlessness is the discipline of governing methods by the specific opponent rather than by habit.** Every repeated method is information handed to the opponent. The heaven-born captain has no fixed form and no repeatable recipe.

moreDetails.gentle: Paragraph 17 describes the mechanism directly: if the opponent strengthens one direction, he weakens the opposite. If he reinforces everywhere, he is weak everywhere. Forcing the opponent into that position is not automatic. It requires presenting threats that the opponent cannot dismiss in multiple directions simultaneously, so that their rational response is always to weaken some sector in order to reinforce another. The mechanism works as long as the threats are credible. A threat the opponent knows you cannot execute is not a real threat, and an opponent who can identify your bluffs can let the weak sector stay weak.
moreDetails.direct: Paragraph 17 describes the forced-defense mechanism with precision: strengthening any one direction weakens the opposite. If the opponent must prepare against attacks in multiple directions, their force at any specific point shrinks proportionately. Forcing the opponent into that condition requires credible threats in multiple directions, which means the mechanism is dependent on having the capacity to actually threaten in more than one direction simultaneously. An opponent who recognizes that your threats in some directions are not executable can concentrate rather than divide, which removes the mechanism's advantage.
moreDetails.competitive: Paragraph 17's mechanism works when the threats forcing the opponent to divide are credible. If the opponent can accurately assess that certain threats are not executable, they can choose not to reinforce the threatened directions and concentrate instead. The mechanism requires not just presenting threats but presenting threats the opponent cannot dismiss. That is both a force requirement and an intelligence requirement: the opponent must be uncertain enough about your actual capabilities in multiple directions that they cannot afford to ignore any of them.

point.gentle: **Numerical weakness comes from having to prepare for attacks from everywhere.** Forcing the opponent into that position, while concentrating your own strength, creates a local superiority that total-force comparisons would not predict.
point.direct: **Forcing the opponent to defend in every direction makes them numerically weak in every direction.** Paragraph 17 describes the mechanism: reinforcing any one direction weakens the opposite. Compelling the opponent into that position is the active application of concentration against division.
point.competitive: **Numerical superiority at the point of contact is created, not inherited.** Force the opponent to defend everywhere, and they are weak everywhere. Concentrate against any one of those weakened points and your fraction of their fraction exceeds theirs at contact.
